## SST gradient magnitude in the simplest useful form

Hey — Pablo here. This page is a **small, checkable skill**: given **one daily SST raster in °C**, compute **|∇SST|** in **°C km⁻¹** the way many movement–environment papers intend—**spatial** centred differences on the grid, not “temperature yesterday minus today.”

We use a **10 × 10** toy grid with a **smooth thermal front** (two water masses meeting) so the gradient map actually looks like something you would expect offshore—not just a boring uniform ramp.

If an AI hands you gradient code, run it on this toy grid first and read the numbers before you trust a real map.

Methods prose for your paper: [`methods.md`](methods.md).

---

## What you are measuring

- **Input:** one 2D SST layer for one day (°C).
- **Output:** |∇SST| at each cell (°C km⁻¹).
- **Not this:** a time slope at a point, a front-probability layer, or a regional mean SST gradient.

---

## Setup




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# terra = fast raster algebra (focal windows, extract, plot) — standard for SST grids.
# pacman::p_load only installs/loads if missing; on this site chunks are frozen for CI.
pacman::p_load(terra)
```
:::


---

## Step 1 — Build a 10 × 10 toy SST field (°C)

**Why:** Real GLORYS cells are tiny; a 10 × 10 grid is still fake data but large enough to **see a front** (high |∇SST| along a boundary) when we plot.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# terra::rast() builds an EMPTY grid: we set columns, rows, geographic extent, and CRS.
# WHY ncols/nrows = 10: more cells → clearer spatial pattern in plots than 3×5.
# WHY EPSG:4326: ordinary longitude/latitude (what CMEMS NetCDF uses).
sst <- terra::rast(
  ncols = 10L,
  nrows = 10L,
  xmin = 170,
  xmax = 171,
  ymin = -45,
  ymax = -44,
  crs = "EPSG:4326"
)

# Build SST in R first (easier to read than nested loops).
# col index = west → east; row index = south → north (see ?terra::values for row order).
sst_mat <- outer(1:10, 1:10, function(row, col) {
  # plogis() makes a smooth step: ~20 °C west, ~21.5 °C east — like a broad thermal front.
  front <- 1.5 * plogis((col - 5.5) * 1.2)
  # Tiny north–south trend so |∇SST| is not literally zero everywhere off the front.
  lat_trend <- 0.008 * row
  20 + front + lat_trend
})

# terra::values() <- fills the raster; byrow = TRUE matches row-major cell order.
terra::values(sst) <- matrix(sst_mat, nrow = 10, ncol = 10, byrow = TRUE)

# Print the grid object: resolution (degrees), extent, CRS — sanity before math.
sst
```

```
resolution  : 0.1, 0.1  (x, y)
```

## Step 2 — Cell size in kilometres

**Why:** Finite differences are in **°C per cell** until we divide by **km per cell**. Skip the cos(lat) step and your |∇SST| is wrong by ~cos(φ) in longitude.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# terra::res() returns cell width in map units (here: degrees lon, degrees lat).
res <- terra::res(sst)

# Mean latitude of all cells — OK on small patches; on huge maps use per-row cos(lat).
clat <- mean(
  terra::yFromCell(sst, seq_len(min(5000L, terra::ncell(sst)))),
  na.rm = TRUE
)

# km per degree longitude SHRINKS toward the poles → multiply by cos(latitude).
dx_km <- as.numeric(res[1]) * 111.32 * cos(clat * pi / 180)
# km per degree latitude is ~111.32 everywhere (small patch: one number is fine).
dy_km <- as.numeric(res[2]) * 111.32

# Named vector prints nicely in the tutorial HTML.
c(dx_km = dx_km, dy_km = dy_km, mean_lat = clat)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
     dx_km      dy_km   mean_lat 
  7.939904  11.132000 -44.500000 
```


:::
:::


At ~0.083° mid-latitude grids, \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta y\) are often **~7–9 km**. Reanalysis SST (e.g. [Copernicus GLORYS12](https://data.marine.copernicus.eu/)) uses similar spacing; always confirm **thetao is °C** in your file (`summary()` ~ 0–35, not ~273–303).

---

## Step 3 — Centred differences → |∇SST|

**Why `terra::focal()`:** It slides a 3×3 window over every cell—exactly what we need for **centred** ∂SST/∂x and ∂SST/∂y without writing nested loops.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sst_grad_magnitude_layer <- function(sst) {
  # Guard: empty raster → stop the recipe early instead of cryptic focal errors.
  if (is.null(sst) || !terra::ncell(sst)) return(NULL)

  res <- terra::res(sst)
  clat <- mean(
    terra::yFromCell(sst, seq_len(min(5000L, terra::ncell(sst)))),
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
  dx_km <- as.numeric(res[1]) * 111.32 * cos(clat * pi / 180)
  dy_km <- as.numeric(res[2]) * 111.32
  if (!is.finite(dx_km) || dx_km <= 0 || !is.finite(dy_km) || dy_km <= 0) return(NULL)

  # 3×3 weights: centre row [-0.5, 0, +0.5] → (T_east - T_west)/2 in °C per half-cell pair.
  w_x <- matrix(c(0, 0, 0, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 0, 0, 0), nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
  # Centre column [-0.5, 0, +0.5] → (T_north - T_south)/2.
  w_y <- matrix(c(0, -0.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.5, 0), nrow = 3, ncol = 3)

  # focal(..., fun = sum) applies the weights; divide by dx_km → °C/km in x.
  # pad = TRUE: fake values at edges so the grid does not shrink (edge cells = noisier).
  gx <- terra::focal(sst, w = w_x, fun = sum, na.rm = TRUE, pad = TRUE) / dx_km
  gy <- terra::focal(sst, w = w_y, fun = sum, na.rm = TRUE, pad = TRUE) / dy_km

  # Pythagoras: magnitude of the 2D gradient vector (always ≥ 0).
  sqrt(gx^2 + gy^2)
}

# Run the function on our toy front — summary() before plot() is the habit.
grad <- sst_grad_magnitude_layer(sst)
summary(grad, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```

 Min.   :0.004118  
 1st Qu.:0.012025  
 Median :0.047595  
 Mean   :0.438194  
 3rd Qu.:0.957914  
 Max.   :1.667691  
```

```{.r .cell-code}
# Side-by-side: WHERE is the front (SST step) vs WHERE |∇SST| peaks (should align).
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(sst, main = "SST (°C)")
plot(grad, main = expression("|"*nabla*SST|" (°C km"^-1*")"))
```

You should see **higher |∇SST|** along the west–east transition (the “front”), not a single uniform colour unless the field were perfectly flat.

## Sanity checks

**Why:** If these fail on toy data, real CMEMS extracts will silently lie to you.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Flat field: multiply by 0 then add 20 → every cell identical → weak gradient (except pad edges).
flat <- sst * 0 + 20

g_flat <- sst_grad_magnitude_layer(flat)
g_ramp <- sst_grad_magnitude_layer(sst)

# terra::global(..., "mean") collapses the raster to one number for quick asserts.
mean_flat <- terra::global(g_flat, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1]
mean_ramp <- terra::global(g_ramp, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1]

stopifnot(is.finite(mean_flat), is.finite(mean_ramp))
# Fronty field must have HIGHER mean |∇SST| than a flat ocean.
stopifnot(mean_ramp > mean_flat, mean_ramp > 0)

c(flat_mean = mean_flat, front_mean = mean_ramp)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 flat_mean front_mean 
 0.4071235  0.4381944 
```


:::
:::


- **Flat SST** → lower mean |∇SST| than the front case (edge padding can add a little noise).  
- **Front SST** → higher mean |∇SST|.  
- If `stopifnot` fires, fix units or stencils before touching Copernicus data.

---

## Common confusions (quick table)

| You might think… | Actually… |
|------------------|-----------|
| “Gradient = SST change over days” | That is a **time** derivative; here we difference **across cells** on one day |
| “Kelvin vs Celsius breaks gradients” | **Differences** are the same size; still keep **one convention** for reporting SST |
| “Coastal |∇SST| = offshore fronts” | Coastal magnitudes often reflect **shore structure**, not open-ocean mesoscale fronts |
| “0.083° sees all fronts” | Mesoscale fronts are **partially** resolved; filaments are not |

---

## Paste-ready Methods sentence

> For each calendar day, |∇SST| (°C km⁻¹) was computed on the native SST grid using centred finite differences; cell sizes were converted to kilometres with 111.32 km per degree of latitude and cosine-adjusted longitude spacing. Gradient magnitude was the Euclidean norm of the horizontal partial derivatives.

More detail: [`methods.md`](methods.md).

---

## Next step (conceptual)

When you link to tracking data: **`terra::extract`** |∇SST| at fix coordinates (same lon/lat convention as your track), then **aggregate** to your model time step (e.g. daily mean). Downloading daily NetCDF from Copernicus is a separate workflow—start from one SST layer you already trust.
